title: Maxwell's Equations
short_intro: Maxwell's equations are a set of four fundamental partial differential equations that formulate the laws of classical electromagnetism. They unify electricity and magnetism and predict the existence of electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Integral and differential forms of Maxwell's equations in free space and simple material media, physical significance of Gauss's law for electricity and magnetism, Faraday's law of induction, and Ampere-Maxwell law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Displacement current derivation, wave equation for electromagnetic waves in free space and conducting media, Poynting vector, energy conservation, boundary conditions for electric and magnetic fields, and electromagnetic potentials.

prerequisites: Vector calculus (Gradient, Divergence, Curl, Stokes' theorem, Divergence theorem)

concept_notes.heading: Gauss's Law for Electricity (Maxwell's First Equation)
bullets: Relates the electric displacement field or electric field to the enclosed free charge density.
Differential form states that the divergence of the electric field is proportional to the local charge density, indicating that electric charges are sources and sinks of electric field lines.
Integral form states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the total charge enclosed divided by the permittivity of free space.

concept_notes.heading: Gauss's Law for Magnetism (Maxwell's Second Equation)
bullets: States that the divergence of the magnetic field is identically zero everywhere.
Implies the non-existence of magnetic monopoles; magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops.
Integral form shows that the net magnetic flux through any closed Gaussian surface is always zero.

concept_notes.heading: Faraday's Law of Induction (Maxwell's Third Equation)
bullets: Relates a time-varying magnetic field to a circulating electric field.
Differential form shows that the curl of the electric field equals the negative time rate of change of the magnetic field vector.
Explains the principle behind electric generators, transformers, and electromagnetic induction.

concept_notes.heading: Ampere-Maxwell Law (Maxwell's Fourth Equation)
bullets: Relates magnetic fields to electric currents and the time rate of change of the electric displacement field.
Maxwell introduced the displacement current term to resolve the inconsistency of Ampere's law for non-steady currents in circuits with capacitors.
Differential form indicates that the curl of the magnetic field is the sum of conduction current density and displacement current density.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Plane Electromagnetic Wave Propagation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Orthogonal sinusoidal waves representing E vector along y-axis and B vector along z-axis, propagating along the x-axis, with arrows indicating cross-product direction E \times B.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates transverse nature of electromagnetic waves where electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding field orientations and wave vector direction.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Charging Capacitor and Displacement Current Loop
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parallel plate capacitor connected to a battery, showing conduction current in wires and a dashed contour loop between capacitor plates passing through the electric field.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that Ampere's law fails without the displacement current term because the contour can be bounded by different surfaces with the same edge.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via theoretical reasoning questions on consistency of Maxwell's equations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hertz's Spark Gap Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An induction coil connected to a spark gap (transmitter) and a distant resonant wire loop with a micro spark gap (receiver).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: First experimental confirmation of the production and detection of high-frequency electromagnetic waves predicted by Maxwell.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Historical and factual multiple-choice questions in PGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: If the electric field in a region is given by E = E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t)\hat{j}, find the corresponding magnetic field B assuming propagation in free space.
solution_steps: Use Faraday's law in differential form: \nabla \times E = -\frac{\partial B}{\partial t}.

Calculate the curl of E: \nabla \times E = \left| \begin{matrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t) & 0 \end{matrix} \right| = \hat{k} \frac{\partial}{\partial x} [E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t)] = k E_0 \cos(kx - \omega t) \hat{k}.
Integrate with respect to time t: B = - \int (k E_0 \cos(kx - \omega t) \hat{k}) dt = \frac{k E_0}{\omega} \sin(kx - \omega t) \hat{k}.
Since \frac{\omega}{k} = c and \frac{1}{c} = \sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}, write B in terms of amplitude B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius R = 0.1 m is being charged with a constant charging current I = 2 A. Calculate the displacement current density through the plates.
solution_steps: The area of the circular plates is A = \pi R^2 = \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.01\pi \text{ m}^2.
The total displacement current in the capacitor equals the conduction current in the connecting wires: I_d = I = 2 \text{ A}.
Displacement current density J_d is given by J_d = \frac{I_d}{A}.

solved_numericals.question: In free space, the magnetic field of an electromagnetic wave is given by B = 10^{-7} \sin(10^7 x - \omega t) \hat{k} \text{ Tesla}. Determine the angular frequency \omega and the electric field amplitude E_0.
solution_steps: From the argument of the sine function, the wave number is k = 10^7 \text{ m}^{-1}.
The relation between angular frequency and wave number for light in free space is \omega = c k.
Substitute c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s} and k = 10^7 \text{ m}^{-1}: \omega = (3 \times 10^8) \times (10^7) = 3 \times 10^{15} \text{ rad/s}.
The relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes is E_0 = c B_0.

assumptions_and_limitations: Maxwell's equations are formulated within the framework of classical macroscopic electrodynamics and do not account for quantum electrodynamic effects at atomic scales.
Material media are assumed to be linear, isotropic, and homogeneous unless tensor permittivities and permeabilities are explicitly introduced.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Displacement current is an actual flow of physical electric charges across the capacitor gap.
common_misconceptions.correct: Displacement current is not a movement of charge, but a term proportional to the time rate of change of the electric field.
common_misconceptions.why: It produces a magnetic field just like conduction current does, but no real charge crosses the dielectric or vacuum gap.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gauss's law for magnetism implies magnetic charges or monopoles exist in pairs.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gauss's law for magnetism states that \nabla \cdot B = 0, proving magnetic monopoles do not exist in classical physics.
common_misconceptions.why: Every magnetic field line is a closed continuous loop with no starting or ending point.

quick_revision: \nabla \times E = -\partial B / \partial t (Changing B induces E)
\nabla \times B = \mu_0 J + \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \partial E / \partial t (Currents and changing E induce B)
Electromagnetic waves are transverse, with c = 1 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}
